citations.quote:
Let $(X,A)$ and $(Y,B)$ be CW pairs with supplied characteristic maps, and let $f:(X,A)\to(Y,B)$ be continuous and cellular on $A$. If $X\setminus A$ has finitely many cells, then, without any choice principle, $f$ is homotopic rel $A$ through maps of pairs to a cellular map $g$, meaning $g(X^n)\subseteq Y^n$ for every $n\ge0$. Assuming the Axiom of Choice, the same conclusion holds for an arbitrary set of relative cells.

If two cellular maps of pairs are homotopic rel $A$, they have a cellular homotopy rel $A$: the homotopy can be taken cellular as a map $X\times I\to Y$ for the product CW structure, with its prescribed end maps. This conclusion is choice-free for a finite relative source and uses AC for an arbitrary relative source. Here cellular homotopy refers to the cylinder map; it does not require every time slice to be cellular on $X$.

Let $K$ be finite, $A\subseteq K$ and $B\subseteq L$ subcomplexes, and $f:(|K|,|A|)\to(|L|,|B|)$ continuous. For all sufficiently large integers $r$, there is a simplicial approximation $g:(\operatorname{sd}^rK,\operatorname{sd}^rA)\to(L,B)$, homotopic as a map of pairs to $f b_K^r$. Here $b_K^r$ is the composite barycentric homeomorphism. No pointwise fixing of a positive-dimensional restriction is asserted.

For continuous $f:X\to Y$ and a commutative unital ring $R$, pullback on singular cohomology satisfies
$$f^*(a\smile b)=f^*a\smile f^*b,\qquad f^*(1)=1.$$
Cup product is associative already on cochains. Consequently $f^*:H^*(Y;R)\to H^*(X;R)$ is a unital graded-ring homomorphism. Homotopic maps give the same homomorphism.

Let $X$ be a space, $R$ a commutative unital ring, $a\in H^p(X;R)$ and $b\in H^q(X;R)$, with $p,q\ge0$. Then
$$a\smile b=(-1)^{pq}b\smile a.$$
The defining cochain operation need not be graded commutative. No AC is required.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Sigma$ be a closed Riemann surface and $m\ge1$. Give $X=\operatorname{Sym}^m(\Sigma)$ its usual complex charts of elementary symmetric coordinates in disjoint support disks. Let $q:\Sigma^m\to X$ be the quotient and $p_i:\Sigma^m\to\Sigma$ its factor projections. For $i<j$ let $\Delta_{ij}=\{z_i=z_j\}$, and put $R=\sum_{i<j}\Delta_{ij}$, with coefficient one on every pair diagonal, including at their intersections. Then there is a holomorphic line-bundle isomorphism
$$q^*\det_{\mathbb C}(TX)\cong\left(\bigotimes_{i=1}^m p_i^*T\Sigma\right)\otimes\mathcal O(R).$$
Under this isomorphism the holomorphic section $\det(dq)$ of
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}\left(\bigotimes_i p_i^*T\Sigma,q^*\det_{\mathbb C}(TX)\right)$$
corresponds to the canonical divisor section of $\mathcal O(R)$. In particular its zero divisor is exactly $R$, even at tuples with three or more equal entries; no transverse-intersection or simple-branch hypothesis is needed for the bundle identity.

Here $\mathcal O(R)$ is constructed by the actual local defining functions in the proof. For a smooth map $F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m):C\to\Sigma^m$ from a closed oriented surface with supplied finite smooth triangle data, the identity implies the degree formula
$$\deg\bigl((qF)^*\det(TX)\bigr)=\sum_i\deg(f_i^*T\Sigma)+\sum_{i<j}\deg\bigl((f_i,f_j)^*\mathcal O(\Delta)\bigr),$$
where $\Delta\subset\Sigma\times\Sigma$ is the ordinary diagonal. Degree means the finite face-winding degree of a complex line bundle. Whenever a pulled-back diagonal section has finitely many isolated zeros, its degree is the sum of their signed local winding indices; at a transverse coincidence this is the sign of $d(f_i-f_j)$ in an oriented surface coordinate. Degrees remain defined if two maps coincide identically.

For $m=1$ the empty divisor has its trivial line and constant section one; $q$ is the identity. For $m=0$ all determinants and tensor products over the one-point symmetric product are trivial and the degree formula is zero. This result does not identify the diagonal class in surface cohomology, compute a sphere's degree, prove a Maslov/domain formula, or realize arbitrary Whitney classes by incidence covers.

derivations.claim: Give each chosen side loop its usual circle coordinate. Map one positive side loop once around $S^1$ and all other loops constantly to one, using the reverse parametrization on its paired negative side. This defines a map of the edge graph to $S^1$. Its composite with the polygon attaching boundary has winding zero, because every side occurs once in each direction. Its argument therefore has a continuous periodic real lift along that boundary: subdivide into finitely many proper circle arcs and concatenate their arguments. Extend that real function over the polygon, for example on a radial collar followed by a constant center, and exponentiate it. This extends the graph map to $\Sigma$. Carry this out for the $2h$ edges to obtain $a_r,b_r$. No infinite selection is used. A circle class can be represented explicitly by assigning to any singular path its lifted argument increment minus the difference of the principal arguments of its endpoints, divided by $2\pi$. The path lift is constructed by finite short-arc subdivisions; refinements give the same lift. On a singular triangle its boundary winding is zero, since the triangle contracts, so this cochain is closed. Thus these maps supply actual integral singular cocycles, without invoking UCT to assert their existence. [given, construct, algebra]

We give the finite line-bundle test used to compute the diagonal class. On any finite CW complex with cells given as characteristic disks, choose a nonzero line section on its one-skeleton by finite vertex/edge interpolation. Over each two-cell choose a disk frame. The winding of this section on its attaching circle is an integer $c(e^2)$. A change of the graph section changes these integers by the cellular coboundary of its edge argument increments; a frame change has zero boundary winding. A line therefore has a well-defined degree-two obstruction cochain modulo these coboundaries. It is a cocycle: on the boundary of a three-cell each oriented edge change cancels, using face frames on its finite boundary subdivision and the fact that the line is trivial on its characteristic three-disk. Conversely, if every two-cell winding is zero, extend the graph section over each two-cell by extending its boundary logarithm; the resulting section is nonzero on the two-skeleton. This is an explicit finite extension, not a line-bundle classification theorem. For a continuous map from a finite closed surface, [F1] makes the map cellular, with homotopy preserving line degree by disk-times-interval frames. Its pullback degree is evaluation of this obstruction cochain on the induced oriented two-cycle. To check this evaluation directly, refine the finite source and target characteristic faces and use [F2] to replace the map by a finite simplicial map. A target face interior point away from all image edges has finitely many inverse affine faces. The graph section extends nonzero off small disks about these inverse points; each remaining boundary winding is the target face winding times its signed affine degree. Sum and cancel the interior edges by [F4]. This proves both the evaluation assertion and its independence of refinements. Thus two line obstruction cochains agreeing on all two-cell generators give equal pullback degrees on every such source. [F1, F2, F4, construct, algebra]

The finite fan computes their products and its signs. Triangulate the polygon from its center. On the block $A_r,B_r,A_r^{-1},B_r^{-1}$, for any two degree-one cocycles $u,v$, let their edge periods be $u_A,u_B,v_A,v_B$. If $t$ is the value of $u$ on the initial radial edge, the cocycle equation gives successive radial values $t,t+u_A,t+u_A+u_B,t+u_B,t$. The front/back cup formula on the four oriented fan triangles consequently contributes $tv_A+(t+u_A)v_B-(t+u_B)v_A-tv_B=u_Av_B-u_Bv_A$. Adjacent radial terms cancel and every paired side is the same singular edge traversed with opposite signs, so the signed fan is a genuine surface cycle. Summing the blocks gives the displayed standard cup matrix. Evaluation of a degree-two class on that cycle determines it on this finite surface: after cellular approximation the cellular chain groups have one face and zero face boundary, since every side exponent sum is zero; the finite cellular cochain differential is also zero. This last comparison uses only finitely many disk deformations from [F1], not an arbitrary singular cycle projection or a UCT splitting. Equivalently the same face-winding test below determines all degree-two classes needed here. The sphere has no one-edges and its single positive face has the same degree-two normalization. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

Apply this test to the finite product CW structure on $\Sigma\times\Sigma$. Its degree-two cells are the two faces $e^2\times v,v\times e^2$ and the $2h\cdot2h$ products of oriented side edges. The cellular boundary is zero in every degree: the surface edge and face boundaries are zero, and the oriented product boundary is $\partial(P\times Q)=\partial P\times Q+(-1)^{\dim P}P\times\partial Q$. This formula follows by orienting each boundary face of its finite characteristic product disks; there is no Kunneth argument. These product disks have finite triangulations, so the test of step1.2 applies. In particular a two-cochain here is completely determined by its values on those finitely many generators. The classes $p_1^*\omega,p_2^*\omega$ evaluate as one on their own face and zero on the other generators. The products $p_1^*u\smile p_2^*v$ evaluate on an edge product $E\times F$ as $u(E)v(F)$: subdivide its oriented square by one diagonal and apply the front/back formula, with the constant vertex terms zero. They vanish on the two face generators. These computations describe the entire degree-two test without a general cross-product isomorphism. [F3, step 2.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

The diagonal line has value one on each face generator. Indeed restrict it to $\Sigma\times\{q\}$ for an interior point $q$, moving the fixed vertex to $q$ by a path if necessary. The section has one simple positive zero at $q$, so [F4] gives degree one; the other factor is identical. For the product of two side loops choose their usual smooth representatives in the polygon handle bands. The $A_r,B_r$ representatives meet once positively in their common handle; different handle bands are disjoint, and like curves have disjoint parallel representatives. These representatives are obtained by joining the paired side midpoints through the polygon bands and rounding their finitely many corners. Moving a representative slightly in its collar gives transverse intersections without changing the loop class. On a product of parameter circles, the diagonal section is locally $z(E(s))-z(F(t))$, with derivative columns $E'(s),-F'(t)$. Hence its signed zero sum is minus the oriented crossing count of the two curves. The values on $A_r\times B_s$ and $B_r\times A_s$ are therefore $-\delta_{rs}$ and $+\delta_{rs}$, and all like-edge products give zero. This computes all the product generators of step3.1, including the case of the same loop, where parallel representatives give zero. [F4, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Steps3.1–4.1 identify the diagonal obstruction cochain with the degree-two class $$p_1^*\omega+p_2^*\omega-\sum_r(p_1^*a_r\smile p_2^*b_r-p_1^*b_r\smile p_2^*a_r).$$ This can also be read purely as equality of its values on the finite two-cell list; step1.2 then proves its pullback degree equality. Pull back by $(f,g)$, use cup naturality [F3], and evaluate on the oriented source cycle. The two face terms are exactly $\deg f,\deg g$ by the signed-face definition of degree and the same finite evaluation test. This gives the asserted formula for arbitrary smooth $f,g$, without requiring their coincidence set to be transverse or finite. [F3, step 1.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

Restrict the diagonal line to the diagonal itself. Its normal complex line is canonically $T\Sigma$: in a surface chart the normal coordinate is $z_1-z_2$, and under $w=h(z)$ its first normal derivative on the diagonal is $h'(z)$, precisely the tangent transition. Thus the derivative of the canonical diagonal section identifies its restricted line with $T\Sigma$. Set $g=f$ in step5.1. By step2.1, naturality and graded commutativity, each pair contributes $\langle f^*(a_r\smile b_r-b_r\smile a_r),[C]\rangle=2\deg f$. Hence its degree is $(2-2h)\deg f$, as claimed. Constant maps have degree zero and zero pulled-back products; $h=0$ is the empty sum; identical maps were treated by a bundle restriction, not an invented finite coincidence count. The only polygon choice was the supplied finite presentation, and all comparisons and extensions used finite cells. This completes the choice-safe diagonal and tangent degree calculation with its stated input scope. [F3, F4, step 2.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra] ∎

boundaries.reason: The Statement assumes closed oriented source and target surfaces, not an empty surface.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and step 6.1 treat h=0 and constant maps.
Step 1.2 uses one face obstruction at a time, and step 4.1 treats each single transverse local crossing.
Statement and step 6.1 treat f=g by line restriction, not a fictitious finite coincidence count.

boundaries.reason: Closed surfaces have no boundary endpoint conditions.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and steps 1.1 through 3.1 use supplied finite polygon and finite-source approximation only; full AC UCT/Kunneth/classification are excluded.

boundaries.reason: The Statement gives a degree formula, not an equivalence.
